newsitem.title: UK: UK markets cheer Pearson's five-year plan.
newsitem.headline: UK markets cheer Pearson's five-year plan.

text.p: British media and leisure company Pearson Plc has regained the confidence of the stock market after setting itself clear performance targets, share analysts said on Tuesday.

Pearson shares added 47.5 pence to 740p on Tuesday, building on Monday's 26.5p gains. The stock has risen more than 11 percent since new management set out its goals in an interim results statement on Monday.

Chief executive Marjorie Scardino, in the job only since January, pledged to deliver annual earnings growth in excess of 10 percent and double the value of the company within five years. Pearson has a market value of some four billion pounds ($6.5 billion).
Analysts welcomed the commitment to consistent earnings growth from a company with a stellar portfolio of assets but a reputation for failing to exploit them to the full.

Broker ABN AMRO Hoare Govett upgraded its recommendation on the stock to "buy" from "hold" on Tuesday. One of its analysts said quality Pearson brands such as the Financial Times newspaper and Penguin books had great potential for improved performance.
"The opportunities are virtually endless. They can do a lot more on both the revenue and the cost side," the analyst said.

Scardino, who heads a management team which has been renewed over the past 18 months, outlined strong growth prospects in the company's Information, Education and Entertainment divisions in presentations on Monday.

She said that Pearson had made some decisions on disposals but gave few hints on what may go. She made it clear that Pearson intends to hang on to its television arm, which makes long-running Australian soap opera "Neighbours".
Analysts said Pearson's remaining indirect stake of four percent in pay television operator BSkyB Plc, worth some 340 million pounds may be sold.
The company said it was considering offers for its Churchill Livingstone medical publishing arm, expected to fetch some 60 million pounds.
Scardino also promised margin improvements. "There is no substitute for elbow grease, managing things a little better," she told reporters.
Pearson reported profit from continuing operations almost doubled to 65.5 million pounds in the first six months of the year, which Scardino said was a "first step" on the road to better performance.
"There are signs they are starting to apply some financial discipline to what had been an asset accumulation business," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
Much of Pearson's business is weighted towards the second half of the year and analysts are forecasting pre-tax profit of around 300 million pounds in 1997.
There was also an almost audible sigh of relief from the investment community that Pearson had not come up with any "nasty surprises".

The latest of these last year emerged when the company took a 100 million pound provision to cover the cost of improper accounting at its Penguin USA subsidiary. The problems dated back to the early 1990s ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
